title: Cost-down, value for money and cost-benefit
moduleNote: High-risk cleaning is excluded from this module on purpose (owner decision, option B, recorded 2026-11-04 in research/OWNER-DECISIONS.md). The high-risk course does not receive PROC-01 to PROC-04. The construction slug was also removed from this module on 2026-11-04 because it has no course folder and is not in passed.json.
audience: Owners, managers and staff in a service business who compare offers, look for savings and approve purchases. The lesson applies whether the purchase is a machine, a service contract or a supply arrangement. Commonwealth officials may also use the value-for-money framework in the Commonwealth Procurement Rules.
referencesAtStart: Official sources used: Commonwealth Procurement Rules 2025 (cover and commencement date 17 November 2025), paragraphs 3.4, 4.4, 4.5 (including 4.5(e) and 4.5(f)) and 4.6; Commonwealth Procurement Rules, value-for-money page, paragraphs 4.4 to 4.6 (no update date shown); Commonwealth Procurement Rules, how to use the rules, paragraphs 3.8 to 3.10 (no update date shown; re-read 2026-11-06). The working definition of value for money and the cost-down and cost-benefit method are general concepts, and have not yet been confirmed as official definitions.
learningOutcomes: Explain value for money as a combination of whole-of-life cost and fit for the stated need, and identify the non-price factors that also count.
List the one-off, running and exit costs that belong in a whole-of-life comparison.
Apply value analysis to a cost-down review without removing a function the outcome still needs.
Prepare a simple cost-benefit analysis for a purchase decision, and record the non-financial benefits separately.

instruction.heading: Value for money is not the lowest price
instruction.body: The Commonwealth Procurement Rules make value for money the core rule of procurement. Paragraph 3.4 calls achieving value for money the core rule of the rules, and it requires consideration of financial and non-financial costs and benefits. Under paragraph 4.4, officials responsible for a procurement must be satisfied, after reasonable enquiries, that the procurement achieves a value for money outcome. Paragraph 4.5 says price is not the sole factor: an official must consider the financial and non-financial costs and benefits of each submission, including quality, fitness for purpose, the supplier's experience, performance and ethical conduct, flexibility and innovation, environmental sustainability and whole-of-life costs. The value-for-money page does not define the term. This lesson uses a working definition: value for money is the best combination of whole-of-life cost and quality for the stated need, judged against the specification. A low price that fails the need is poor value. A higher price that meets the need at a lower total cost can be the better buy. Record the judgement and its reasons, so that another person can see why the choice was made.

instruction.heading: Whole-of-life cost
instruction.body: Whole-of-life cost is the total cost of owning and using an item or service over its life, and the purchase price is only one part of it. Paragraph 4.6 of the rules gives examples, including maintenance and operating costs, transition-out costs, licensing costs, and decommissioning, remediation and disposal costs. For a small business the same idea applies. Running costs include consumables, energy, servicing and insurance. Training people to use the item is a cost. The cost of getting out of the arrangement, such as moving to another supplier or removing equipment at the end, is also a cost. Total acquisition cost is a narrower idea that adds delivery, installation and set-up costs to the price. The gap between the cheapest quote and the lowest whole-of-life cost often sits in running and exit costs, which are easy to overlook when comparing quotes on the first page.

instruction.heading: Cost-down and value analysis
instruction.body: Cost-down is the deliberate reduction of the cost of a product or service without losing the function the business needs. It can be done by changing the specification, for example by accepting a material that performs the same function at a lower cost, or by changing the way the work is delivered. Value analysis asks three questions about each element: what function it performs, what it costs, and whether another element could perform the same function for less. Removing an item from the specification can be a valid cost-down step, but only after the function it performs has been identified and confirmed as unnecessary, or moved to another item. Removing a function the outcome still needs produces failure, rework or disputes, and those costs can exceed the saving. Repeating the current contract and waiting for the market to deliver a lower price is not cost-down. It leaves the cost choices untouched. A cost-down review is strongest when it starts from the specification and the whole-of-life picture, because that is where the real cost choices sit.

instruction.heading: Cost-benefit analysis for a purchase decision
instruction.body: A cost-benefit analysis compares the quantified costs and benefits of a decision over a stated period. List every cost: the price, set-up and transition costs, training, trial periods, running costs, maintenance and the cost of exit. Then list every benefit that can be measured in money, such as savings in consumables, fewer call-backs or less downtime. Benefits that cannot be measured in money, such as lower environmental impact or reduced risk to staff, should be recorded separately, with the reason, rather than forced into a dollar figure. Where one supplier could stop supply, a contingency source or extra stock has a cost too. Put that cost in the analysis as a risk line, state how often a failure might happen as an assumption, and record where the assumption came from. Test the result against the assumptions that matter most, and note what result would change the decision. Scale the analysis to the purchase. A detailed study of a small item can cost more than it saves. Paragraph 4.4(e) asks that the effort put into a procurement fit its size and breadth.

procedure: Write the need and the specification, and confirm the outcome the purchase must achieve.
List each offer's purchase price, then add set-up, transition, training and trial costs.
Estimate running, maintenance and exit costs over the period of use. State each estimate as an assumption with its source or basis.
Compare the offers on whole-of-life cost, then record the non-financial factors on which they differ, such as quality, risk and environmental impact.
Test the result against the assumptions that matter most, and note the change that would alter the decision.
Record the decision, the value-for-money reasons and a review date in the purchase file.

workedExamples.situation: Invented example figures, not market prices: a business chooses between two floor-cleaning machines for a five-year period. Machine A costs an invented $4,000 to buy, with an invented running cost of $1,200 a year. Machine B costs an invented $5,200 to buy, with an invented running cost of $600 a year. Both meet the specification. Disposal and switching costs are left out for simplicity.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which machine gives better value for money on whole-of-life cost over five years, and what is the difference?
workedExamples.reasoning: Machine A over five years is $4,000 plus five times $1,200, which is $10,000. Machine B is $5,200 plus five times $600, which is $8,200. On this basis Machine B is $1,800 cheaper over the period. If both machines meet the specification equally, Machine B gives better value for money. The decision should be checked against the assumptions: if the running-cost estimate for Machine B is wrong, the answer may change, so the estimate and its source should be recorded.

workedExamples.situation: Invented example figures, not market prices: a business is considering a new chemical supplier. The one-off switching cost is an invented $900 for staff training and a trial period. The new supplier is estimated to save an invented $1,500 a year on chemicals. The analysis covers three years.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the net benefit over three years, and how should a quality concern be recorded?
workedExamples.reasoning: Three years of savings is $4,500. Subtracting the one-off switching cost of $900 gives a net benefit of $3,600 over three years, before any quality risk. A quality risk that cannot be put in money terms should be recorded as a separate non-financial factor, and the trial period is the step that reduces it. If a quality failure would cost money, estimate that cost as its own line, and state its likelihood as an assumption.

equipmentAndPpe: A whole-of-life comparison worksheet with columns for one-off, running and exit costs, and an assumptions column with sources.
Two or more written offers for the same specification, put on the same scope and period.
No personal protective equipment is needed for this desk-based lesson.

commonErrors.error: Equating value for money with the lowest price.
commonErrors.prevention: Compare offers on whole-of-life cost and fit for the stated need, and record the reasons for the choice.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out switching, training and exit costs.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a checklist of one-off and exit costs for every comparison, and mark any item not applicable with a reason.

commonErrors.error: Cutting a feature without confirming the function it performs.
commonErrors.prevention: Identify the function first, then check whether the outcome still holds without it.

commonErrors.error: Comparing offers with different scopes, volumes or periods.
commonErrors.prevention: Put every offer on the same scope, volume and period before comparing totals.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This lesson explains general value-for-money reasoning and is not legal advice. Paragraphs 3.8 to 3.10 of the Commonwealth Procurement Rules (2025 instrument, commencing 17 November 2025) set out which Commonwealth entities and officials must comply with paragraphs 4.4, 4.5 and 4.6. The rules do not mention private businesses, so this lesson makes no claim that they bind a private business. The value-for-money page on finance.gov.au shows no update date of its own. Sources:, and.

The finance.gov.au landing page for the rules shows a version dated 14 December 2020, which conflicts with the 2025 instrument that commences on 17 November 2025. This lesson uses the 2025 instrument.
Confirm it with a registered tax agent before relying on any after-tax figure.

qualityStandard: The decision compares offers on whole-of-life cost and non-financial factors, not on price alone.
Every one-off, running and exit cost is listed, or recorded as not applicable with a reason.
Each estimate is labelled as an assumption, with its source or the basis for it.
The decision record states the result, the assumption that would change it and a review date.
documentationEvidence: Whole-of-life or cost-benefit worksheet with dates, assumptions and sources.
Decision record stating the value-for-money reasons and the non-financial factors considered.
summary: Value for money is the best combination of whole-of-life cost and fit for the stated need. The lowest price is not automatically the best value.
Whole-of-life cost includes running, transition and disposal costs, and these often decide the comparison.
Cost-down must protect the function the outcome needs. A cost-benefit analysis counts one-off switching costs and records non-financial benefits separately.

knowledgeChecks.question: Two offers are for the same service. One has a lower purchase price but high running and exit costs. Which basis is better for judging value for money?
options: Whole-of-life cost and fit for the stated need
The lowest up-front price, since it is paid first

knowledgeChecks.question: Which cost is most likely to be a whole-of-life cost for the buyer?
options: A one-off discount on the first order from the supplier
Costs of moving to another supplier when the arrangement ends
A commission the supplier pays its own sales staff

knowledgeChecks.question: A review finds a feature that appears to do no useful work. What is the right next step before a cost-down change?
options: Remove it at once to capture its full price saving today from the job and the supplier
Keep it, because any change is a risk to the outcome of the whole job and the client
Confirm the function it serves, then remove or change it only if the outcome still holds

knowledgeChecks.question: In a cost-benefit analysis of changing supplier, which item must be included?
options: Only the benefits, so the case looks simpler to the owner
Only the lowest unit price on the new offer and the quote
One-off switching costs such as training and a trial period
